per_question.answer: The minimum length for a password used as a single-factor authentication mechanism is 15 characters [2]. This requirement is specified for verifiers and CSPs under the password verifier requirements [2].

When a password is used only as part of multi-factor authentication, it must be a minimum of eight characters in length [1]. Verifiers and CSPs may allow shorter passwords than single-factor ones, but not below this eight-character minimum [1]. This requirement is specified in the password verifier rules under Sec. 3.1.1.2 [1].

Verifiers and CSPs SHALL NOT impose other composition rules (e.g., requiring mixtures of different character types) for passwords [2]. The only length requirements are a minimum of 15 characters for single-factor use, or 8 characters for multi-factor use [1]. No other composition rules may be imposed [2].

No, verifiers and CSPs SHALL NOT require subscribers to change passwords periodically [1][2]. However, they SHALL force a change if there is evidence that the authenticator has been compromised [1][2].
The minimum length of a look-up secret is at least six decimal digits (or equivalent) in length [1][2]. This requirement is specified for look-up secret authenticators and verifiers [1][2].

A secret from a look-up secret authenticator SHALL be used successfully only once [1]. This means each secret can be used exactly one time [1]. The source also notes that if the secret is derived from a grid card, each grid cell SHOULD be used only once [1].

Email is prohibited for out-of-band authentication because it may be vulnerable to access using only a password, interception in transit or at intermediate mail servers, and rerouting attacks such as DNS spoofing [1][2]. This prohibition does not apply to confirmation codes sent to validate email addresses or issued as recovery codes, as those are not authentication processes [1].
The authentication SHALL be considered invalid unless completed within 10 minutes [3]. This requirement applies to out-of-band authentication processes [3].

The verifier shall limit consecutive failed authentication attempts using a specific authenticator on a single subscriber account to no more than 100 by disabling that authenticator [4]. This limit of 100 attempts is an upper bound, and agencies may impose lower limits [4]. If more than one authenticator is involved with an excessive number of attempts, both authenticators shall be disabled [4]. Disabled authenticators must be rebound to the subscriber account to be usable again [4].

The maximum overall reauthentication timeout at AAL2 is no more than 24 hours, as stated in the AAL2 reauthentication requirements [1]. This is a "SHOULD" recommendation, not a strict "SHALL" requirement, but it establishes the definite overall timeout limit [1]. The general session management rules confirm that when either the overall or inactivity timeout expires, the session must be terminated [2].

The recommended inactivity timeout at AAL3 is no more than 15 minutes [1]. This is stated as a "SHOULD" requirement, meaning it is a recommendation rather than a strict mandate [1]. The overall reauthentication timeout at AAL3 must be no more than 12 hours [1].

Session-binding secrets must be at least 64 bits in length [2]. This requirement is listed among the mandatory properties for secrets used for session binding, which also include being established during or immediately following authentication and generated using an approved random bit generator [2].
Session monitoring is sometimes called continuous authentication [1].

The question asks for the entropy requirement of a saved recovery code. According to the source on page 58, under section 4.2.1.1, the recovery code must include at least 64 bits from an approved random bit generator [1]. This directly answers the question about the required entropy.

A saved recovery code must include at least 64 bits of entropy from an approved random bit generator [1].

For every account recovery event, a notification must be sent to the subscriber or their designee [3]. This notification is intended to help detect fraudulent use of account recovery [1]. The notification must be sent to all stored notification addresses except postal addresses, unless specific exceptions apply, such as when the only other address is where an issued recovery code was sent [2]. These notifications provide clear instructions and contact information in case the recipient repudiates the event [2].

The biometric system SHALL operate with a false match rate (FMR) of one in 10000 or better for all demographic groups [1]. This FMR must be achieved under the conditions of a conformant attack, defined as a zero-effort impostor attempt [1]. The system must also be configured with a fixed threshold, as changing it for each demographic is not feasible [1].

No. Biometric characteristics cannot be used for single-factor authentication and must be combined with a physical authenticator as part of multi-factor authentication [3]. The guidelines explicitly state that biometrics "SHALL only be used as part of multi-factor authentication with a physical authenticator" [2]. Additionally, an alternative non-biometric authentication option must always be provided to the subscriber [2]. Biometrics do not constitute secrets and therefore cannot serve as standalone authenticators [3].

At AAL2, when two single-factor authenticators are used, the combination must include one physical authenticator (something you have) from a specified list, used together with either a password or a biometric comparison [1]. The permitted physical authenticators listed are a look-up secret, an out-of-band device, or a single-factor OTP [1]. The source text cuts off after listing single-factor OTP, so the full list of permitted physical authenticators is not completely visible in the provided excerpt [1].

The Identity Assurance Level (IAL) refers to identity proofing functions [1]. It describes the robustness of the identity proofing process used to determine the identity of an individual [3]. IAL reflects the level of assurance that an applicant holds the claimed real-life identity [4].

AAL refers to authentication functions within the digital identity assurance framework [3]. More specifically, it describes the robustness of the authentication process itself and the binding between an authenticator and a specific individual’s identifier [4]. The AAL is selected to mitigate risks that result from potential authentication failures [4]. It also reflects the level of assurance that the claimant is the same individual to whom the authenticator was registered [5]. Stronger authentication, meaning a higher AAL, requires malicious actors to expend greater resources to subvert the process [2].

The Federation Assurance Level (FAL) refers to federation functions when the relying party (RP) is connected to a credential service provider (CSP) or an identity provider (IdP) through a federated protocol [2]. It describes the robustness of the federation process used to communicate authentication and attribute information to an RP from an IdP, and is selected to mitigate risks from potential federation failures [3]. A FAL is a category that describes the process used in a federation transaction to communicate authentication events and subscriber attributes to an RP [4].

To achieve AAL2, proof of possession and control of two distinct authentication factors is required through secure authentication protocols [1][2]. Approved cryptographic techniques are required [2][5]. Applications assessed at AAL2 must offer a phishing-resistant authentication option [1]. Authentication must use either a multi-factor authenticator or a combination of two separate authentication factors [5].

An AAL3 authenticator must use a non-exportable private key [1][2]. This key must be part of a cryptographic authenticator that provides phishing resistance [1]. The private key must be stored in a hardware-protected, isolated environment to prevent it from being leaked [3]. Specifically, non-exportable authentication keys suitable for AAL3 must be stored in an isolated execution environment protected by hardware or in a separate processor with a controlled interface [5].

IAL3 requires a trained CSP representative (proofing agent) to interact directly with the applicant during an on-site attended identity proofing session, and it requires the collection of at least one biometric [1]. IAL1 only validates core attributes against authoritative or credible sources, while IAL2 requires additional evidence and a more rigorous validation process, but neither includes these direct-interaction or biometric requirements [1]. IAL3 also targets sophisticated attacks, advanced evidence falsification, theft, repudiation, and advanced social engineering, unlike the lower levels [2].
A claimant is a subject whose identity is to be verified using one or more authentication protocols [1][4].

A verifier is an entity that confirms the claimant’s identity by verifying the claimant’s possession and control of one or more authenticators using an authentication protocol [2]. To do this, the verifier needs to confirm the binding of the authenticators with the subscriber account and check that the subscriber account is active [2]. This definition is consistent across the guidelines, where the verifier’s role is described identically in the terminology section [4].

The Pass Rate (Overall) metric measures the "Percentage of unique users who successfully complete identity proofing" [1]. This metric is categorized under the "Proofing" type [1]. The document specifies that "all references to unique users include both legitimate users and imposters" [2].

RPs and CSPs SHALL enable individuals to convey grievances and seek redress through an issue handling process that is documented, accessible, trackable, and usable by all individuals, with instructions easy to find on a public-facing website [1]. This process must include a governance model with documented roles and responsibilities, and it must be implemented as a dedicated function that impartially reviews evidence, collects additional evidence, and expeditiously resolves issues and determines corrective action [1]. Human support personnel must be available to intervene and override algorithmic adjudication outputs, and support personnel must be educated on issue handling procedures, avenues for redress, and alternatives to gain access to services [1]. Organizations must also implement a process for personnel and technologies to report and address major barriers and grievances, and incorporate findings into continuous evaluation and improvement activities [1].

Organizations must document all uses of AI/ML and communicate them to relying organizations, with CSPs, IdPs, or verifiers disclosing integrated AI/ML use to all RPs making access decisions [1]. They must also provide information on training methods and techniques, training data sets, model update frequency, and testing results to entities using their technology [1]. Organizations should implement the NIST AI Risk Management Framework to evaluate risks introduced by such systems [1]. Finally, they must perform and document privacy risk assessments for personal information and data processed by AI/ML systems [3].

A credential service provider (CSP) is a trusted entity whose functions include identity proofing applicants to the identity service and registering authenticators to subscriber accounts [1]. It also enrolls applicants into its identity service, establishes subscriber accounts, and binds authenticators to those accounts [2]. A subscriber account is the CSP’s established record of the subscriber, the subscriber’s attributes, and associated authenticators [2]. The CSP issues, stores, and maintains the credential, which binds an identity to at least one authenticator possessed and controlled by a subscriber [1]. A CSP may be an independent third party [1].

Verifiers and CSPs should permit a maximum password length of at least 64 characters [1]. This is stated as a SHOULD requirement in the password verifier rules [1]. The guideline aims to avoid excessive complexity that frustrates users [3]. Therefore, the minimum upper limit to allow is 64 characters [1].

The provided documents do not state whether a verifier may check only part of a submitted password. The sources address password length, composition rules, storage, and transmission, but not partial verification [1][2][4]. Therefore, I don't know based on the provided documents.

The salt used when hashing passwords must be at least 32 bits in length [1]. It should also be chosen to minimize salt value collisions among stored hashes [1]. This requirement applies to both passwords and look-up secrets [1][5].

If the subscriber entered an identifier, the binding code must be at least 40 bits in length [1]. This is the lower of the two thresholds, since the alternative case without an identifier requires at least 112 bits [1]. The code must be generated using an approved random bit generator and is usable only once for a maximum of 10 minutes [1].

A service should compare the proposed passphrase against a blocklist of unacceptable passwords [1]. This blocklist should include passwords from previous breach corpuses, dictionary words used as passwords, and specific words such as the name of the service itself that users are likely to choose [1]. The dictionary only needs to include entries that meet the minimum length requirement [1].

The login screen should offer an option to display the password rather than masking it with dots or asterisks while it is entered [2]. It may also show each typed character briefly to confirm correct entry, which is common on mobile devices [2]. The screen should allow at least 10 entry attempts and provide clear feedback on errors and remaining attempts [3].

The documents do not directly state whether syncable authenticators are permitted at the highest assurance level. They do establish that syncable authenticators—those that copy authentication secrets to a sync fabric—must meet specific requirements, including encryption of keys with at least 112-bit security strength and AAL2-equivalent MFA for access to the sync fabric [2]. The document also notes that these requirements are detailed in Appendix B [4]. However, no source explicitly addresses whether such authenticators can be used at AAL3 or the highest assurance level. No. A PIN and a password are both "something you know" factors, so requesting both does not combine distinct authentication factors [5]. Multi-factor authentication requires proof of possession and control of two distinct authentication factors [5]. NIST describes multi-factor authenticators as combining "something you have" with either "something you know" or "something you are" [1][2]. Therefore, a PIN plus a password remains single-factor authentication.

According to the AAL summary table, AAL3 must require phishing resistance in addition to verifier compromise protections [1]. The table lists the AAL3 control objective as "Require phishing resistance and verifier compromise protections" [1].

The term is **authentication intent**, defined as the process of confirming the claimant’s intent to authenticate by requiring user intervention, serving as a countermeasure against malware at the endpoint [1].
